claims.text: Rapid heating and cooling frequently produces noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with phase separation.
Rapid heating and cooling frequently produces elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid heating and cooling frequently produces irregular particle morphology or high thermal decomposition in these nanoparticles.
The controlled intervention is a precisely timed isothermal hold at an intermediate temperature while retaining the rest of the rapid thermal cycle.
The hold temperature should be below the maximum synthesis temperature but high enough to produce measurable atomic diffusion.
An intermediate isothermal hold enhances atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility during the hold reduces local compositional fluctuations.
Enhanced atomic mobility permits uniform short-range order to form.
Reduced compositional fluctuations and uniform short-range order mediate nucleation of the desired single-phase solid solution.
Insufficient time for atomic rearrangement during rapid heating and cooling causes compositional inhomogeneity and phase separation.
The isothermal hold supplies diffusion time that smooths compositional fluctuations.
Diffusion during the hold eliminates the driving force for phase segregation and improves control over crystal-structure selection.
Relative to the no-hold baseline, the intermediate hold will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to the no-hold baseline, the intermediate hold will produce more uniform particle morphology.
Relative to the no-hold baseline, the intermediate hold will produce a more consistent single-phase crystal structure.
Reduced phase impurities may lower the thermal decomposition temperature.

The proposed effect applies to noble metal–based alloys containing more than five elements under rapid thermal processing, with the effective hold conditions depending on composition, particle size, and elemental diffusion rates.
